title: GPU siloing: adaptive minimum throughput and eviction orchestration
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Objective: Implement a GPU siloing system that enforces per-tenant minimum throughput guarantees while enabling graceful, policy-driven eviction when tenants exceed contracted burst allowances. The feature must integrate with our autoscaler, respect latency SLOs, and provide clear telemetry for cost and impact attribution.

Scope:
- Define tenant "silo profiles" (min guaranteed tokens/sec, burst window, priority) stored in control plane.
- Enforce min-throughput using a lightweight admission controller and rate-aware batching placement so guaranteed requests are scheduled on reserved lanes.
- Build eviction orchestration that uses score-based eviction (combining burst debt, historical SLO breaches, and priority) and supports soft-preempt (throttle) then hard-evict (preempt KV + pause) paths.
- Integrate with autoscaling policies: autoscaler should consider active guaranteed capacity so dedicated scaling isn't starved by noisy bursts.
- Expose tenant-level telemetry: guaranteed vs actual throughput, eviction events, latency delta, and billing deltas.
- Admin APIs/console controls to adjust silo profiles, run emergency quarantine, and view live evacuation plans.

Acceptance criteria:
- 99% of guaranteed requests meet token/sec contracts under mixed workloads in 4-node canary lab.
- Eviction path triggers within 60s of proven burst policy violation and reduces noisy-tenant impact by >= 80% for victims' p95 latency.
- Autoscaler respects guaranteed reserved capacity within 5% and does not scale down reserved lanes below configured min.
- Console shows per-tenant eviction reason and a link to the associated playbook.

Design decisions and trade-offs:
- Chosen approach is lane-based (soft partitions) rather than hard hardware slicing to balance utilization vs isolation. Hard slicing (exclusive GPU assignment) gives stronger isolation but reduces utilization for low duty-cycle tenants; lane-based allows statistical multiplexing with enforced guarantees.
- Eviction uses a two-stage strategy: soft-throttle first (limits batching share and concurrency) then hard-preempt if throttling fails. This reduces customer-visible failures but complicates implementation of KV state migration.
- Admission controller is implemented in the request router to avoid extra RPCs during scheduling; this introduces additional complexity in router state but keeps enforcement latency low.

Risks and mitigations:
- KV cache loss on hard preempt: mitigation is to checkpoint hot KV segments to local SSD and rely on fast rebuild lanes; add a preempt handshake to give a 2s drain window.
- Incorrect scoring may evict wrong tenants: mitigation includes a replayable eviction decision log and conservative initial thresholds.
- Autoscaler oscillation: mitigation uses hysteresis windows and weight reserved capacity as sticky for 5 minutes post-scale.

Operational runbook highlights:
- Dashboard alert "SiloEviction:HighRate" triggers on >3 evictions/min for same host; recommended action: increase reserved lanes or throttle offending tenant.
- Console action "Quarantine tenant" will mark tenant read-only for 10m and trigger immediate eviction orchestration.

Integrations and links:
- Confluence spec: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/234512345/GPU+Siloing+Design
- Prototype notebook (perf experiments): drive://redwood-shared/gpu-siloing/prototype_v2.ipynb
- Draft RFC: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rfcs/pull/184
- Canary dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.company/d/eviction/gpu-siloing-canary

Metrics to watch: guaranteed_throughput_ratio, eviction_count, p95_latencies_by_tenant, autoscale_adjustments, KV_rebuild_time
